Currying
How a curried JavaScript function waits for all of its arguments, how to curry by hand and with curry, use it in composition and build specialized functions.

Understand how a curried function postpones evaluation until it has all of its arguments, and learn to curry functions by hand and with curry to use them in composition and build specialized functions.
text

Currying is one of the techniques used in functional programming, in which the function is evaluated only once all of its arguments have been supplied, while given only some of the arguments the function returns a new function.
Currying can be used:
list
In function composition, when a function in a chain of calls expects two or more arguments.
When we want to create specialized functions based on a base function by changing the value of an argument captured in a closure.
code
So how do we curry an arbitrary function with n parameters whose values we don't know — for example, a function with 5 or more parameters?

We can automatically curry any function with a fixed number of parameters and pass it the arguments in any grouping: one at a time or several per call. Only the grouping changes; the order of the arguments stays the same.
Now let's look at the full power of currying through examples of function composition.
We can also create specialized functions with the help of currying. It is somewhat similar to "inheritance" in OOP.
We take a base curried function, and then we build other functions through calls. Enough theory — let's get straight to the examples.
A curried function is evaluated only once it has all of its arguments; given only some of them, it returns a new function.
Currying is used in function composition, when a function in a chain of calls expects two or more arguments, and to create specialized functions based on a base function.
Any function with a fixed number of parameters can be curried automatically and given its arguments in any grouping: only the grouping changes, the order of the arguments stays the same.
Specialized functions are built from a base curried function through calls: equalByStatus from equalBy, then isOnline from equalByStatus. This is somewhat similar to "inheritance" in OOP.

Write a curried function formatLog :: String -> String -> String -> String by hand: it takes a level, a module name and a message and returns a string like [ERROR] auth: wrong password. Build specialized functions from it: logError and logInfo with the level fixed, and from those, authError and cartInfo with the module fixed. Use them to print the messages from the starter.

[ERROR] auth: wrong password
[ERROR] auth: token expired
[INFO] cart: item added

applyDiscount(percent, price) expects two arguments, while map hands the function one price at a time. Curry it with curry from Ramda, fix a 10% discount and use pipe to build totalWithDiscount: it takes the prices of the order items, applies the discount to each of them and adds them up.
